newsitem.title: USA: OMB chief says Congress' D.C. plan goes too far.
newsitem.headline: OMB chief says Congress' D.C. plan goes too far.

text.p: OMB's chief signaled Monday that Congress went too far in slashing the role of District of Columbia elected officials in its new financial bailout law for the city.

Franklin Raines, director of the Office of Managment and Budget, said the administration will take "immediate" steps to try to restore some authority, at least to the District's 13-member city council.
Raines made the comments at a press briefing following a meeting between D.C.'s delegate to Congress Eleanor Holmes Norton and President Clinton at the White House.

Norton asked for the meeting because a historic D.C. rescue package approved by Congress rips authority over nine key city agencies away from D.C. Mayor Marion Barry and gives it to the city's two-year-old financial control board.
The controversial transfer was engineered by Sen. Lauch Faircloth, R-N.C., chairman of the Senate Appropriations Committee's subpanel on D.C.

Last week, control board chief Andrew Brimmer enraged Norton, Barry and the city counsel by barring Barry from acting without his permission and telling heads of nine major city agencies to report to him only.
Raines told reporters that the law's transfer of authority to the control board was "an unnecessary appendage" to the D.C. bailout package, which had originated at the White House.

"Our position from the beginning was that there was no need for the Congress to legislate...management changes," Raines said. "We now have to see that (the new law) is implemented in a way that is as respectful of home rule as possible."
Home rule refers to authority granted to D.C. by Congress in 1994 to elect its own mayor and city council.
Norton said of Monday's session with Clinton, "The President was clear that he will help me in whatever way we can to try to begin the process of getting back the home rule we have lost."
Raines said the White House will look at "immediate measures, such as restoring the ability of the city counsel to have a role in the confirmation of department heads."
He did not mention restoring that role for D.C.'s Mayor Barry who has called the Faircloth amendment a "rape" of democracy in the District.
Raines said the White House also will look at "other items" to make sure that the policymaking role of D.C.'s elected officials are "respected in this process."
But Raines also urged the various players to set the good of D.C. above other concerns.
"I know there are disappointments in this bill for some parties. But I hope personal disappointments don't get in the way of the concerns of the city as a whole," he said.
Norton said she and Rep. Tom Davis, R-Va., met last Friday with control board chief Andrew Brimmer and plan meetings with Barry and city counsel chair later this week.

"The point of those meetings is to seek the greatest collaboration possible between the control board and elected officials," Norton, a Democrat, said. "We are very pleased that Mr. Brimmer seemed to agree that is the approach that should be taken."
